claim: A 4th-century Chinese first-aid handbook told readers to soak a handful of qinghao (sweet wormwood) in water and drink the juice for fevers. In the 1970s Tu Youyou read that line and it led her team to artemisinin, now a frontline malaria drug.
evidence: A handful of qinghao immersed with 2 liters of water, wring out the juice and drink it all
source: Tu Y. The discovery of artemisinin (qinghaosu) and gifts from Chinese medicine. Nature Medicine 17(10): 1217-1220, 2011
locator: quoting Ge Hong, Zhouhou Beiji Fang (Handbook of Prescriptions for Emergencies)
author: Tu Youyou
licence: Copyright; quote one short credited line only
caveat: Tu won the 2015 Nobel Prize for this. Modern artemisinin drugs are purified and dosed; drinking wormwood juice is NOT a malaria treatment. Historical interest only, not medical advice. Some traditional remedies are toxic.
use_in: Deep dive candidate: 1,600 years from a handbook to a Nobel

claim: Her breakthrough came from reading the old recipe closely: it used cold water, not boiling. Heat was destroying the active compound, so her team switched to low-temperature extraction.
evidence: extraction at a lower temperature might be necessary to preserve antimalarial activity
author: Tu Youyou
caveat: Fragment of a longer sentence. Historical interest only, not medical advice. Some traditional remedies are toxic.
use_in: Reel: 'The answer was in how they made it, not what'

claim: China's oldest surviving materia medica lists 365 medicines and sorts them into three grades by their effects and how toxic they are.
evidence: This text records 365 medicinals and summarizes medicinal experiences up to the Han Dynasty.
source: Zhao Z, Guo P, Brand E. A concise classification of bencao (materia medica). Chinese Medicine 13:18, 2018
author: Zhao, Guo, Brand
caveat: The book is attributed to the mythical 'Divine Farmer' Shennong; it was compiled by unknown authors around the Han period. Grades = high/medium/low by effect and toxicity. Historical interest only, not medical advice. Some traditional remedies are toxic.
use_in: Carousel: how the oldest drug list was organised

claim: Li Shizhen spent 27 years writing the Bencao Gangmu, a huge Ming-dynasty compendium of medicines; UNESCO lists it as world documentary heritage.
evidence: Compiled and written by LI Shi-zhen (1518~1593), a medical expert of the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644) over a period of 27 years.
source: UNESCO Silk Roads: Ben Cao Gang Mu (Compendium of Materia Medica)
author: UNESCO
caveat: First draft completed 1578; printed after his death (c. 1593-96). Entry counts (often given as 1,892) not checked yet. Historical interest only, not medical advice. Some traditional remedies are toxic.

claim: In 1330 Hu Sihui, dietician at the Mongol Yuan court, wrote the Yinshan Zhengyao, a food-as-medicine manual drawing on Chinese, Mongol and Arab sources.
evidence: Hu Sihui incorporated a wide variety of dietary and medical knowledge from Chinese, Mongol, and Arab sources for his work.
source: Medievalists.net (Sept 2024) summarising Niu H. et al., Yinshan Zhengyao: exploring the power of food and inheriting healthy thoughts. Food & Medicine Homology, 2024
author: Niu, Aruhan, Surenjidiin, Zhang, Zhang, Li
caveat: Read the journal article itself before posting counts (232 foods, 174 medicinal plants come from the summary). English translation: Buell & Anderson, A Soup for the Qan. Historical interest only, not medical advice. Some traditional remedies are toxic.
use_in: Reel: 'The Mongol emperor had a dietician'

claim: Under the Mongol Ilkhans, the vizier Rashid al-Din had a Chinese medical book translated into Persian, the Tanksuqname. Only the first of its four volumes survives, in Istanbul.
evidence: The Tānksūqnāme was translated by order of Faḍl-Allah Rashīd al-Dīn Ibn ʿImād al-Dawla Abū al-Khayr (1247-1318).
source: Acıduman A, Şems Ş, Arda B, Kırilen G. A Preliminary Study on Chapters Related to Human Anatomy in an Illustrated Persian Medical Book: Tānksūqnāme. Belleten 87(309): 415-437, 2023
author: Acıduman et al.
caveat: Copy made in Tabriz, 10 December 1313; Ayasofya 3596, Süleymaniye Library. Genuine 'lost knowledge': three volumes are gone.
use_in: Reel: 'Three volumes of this book are missing'

claim: Ibn al-Baytar, a botanist born in Málaga, compiled a dictionary of about 1,400 simple medicines from plants, animals and minerals.
evidence: se enumeran alrededor de 1400 simples de origen vegetal, animal y mineral.
source: Cabo-González AM. El Kitāb Mīzān al-Ṭabīb de Ibn al-Bayṭār. Folia Orientalia LVI, 2019
author: Ana M. Cabo-González
caveat: Evidence sentence is Spanish; translate on the post. Dates c. 1180/1187-1248. The big work is Kitāb al-Jāmiʿ. Historical interest only, not medical advice. Some traditional remedies are toxic.
use_in: Deep dive candidate: the Andalusian botanist

claim: Al-Zahrawi of Córdoba wrote a thirty-volume medical encyclopedia and drew the surgical instruments he used, probably the first illustrations of their kind.
evidence: He included illustrations of the surgical instruments, probably the first of their kind
source: Manaf F. Abulcasis, the pharmacist surgeon. Hektoen International 7(1), Winter 2015
author: Fadlurrahman Manaf
caveat: Hektoen is a medical-humanities journal, not peer-reviewed research; confirm '200 instruments' against a scholarly edition (Spink & Lewis 1973) before a deep dive.

claim: Ibn Zuhr of Seville tested a tracheotomy on a goat to show it was safe before anyone tried it on people.
evidence: performed experimentally a tracheotomy on a goat, proving the safety of this operation in humans
source: Karamanou M. et al. Avenzoar's (1091-1162) clinical description of cancer. JBUON 20(4): 1171-1174, 2015
author: Karamanou, Tsoucalas, Saridaki, Iavazzo, Androutsos
caveat: Same paper says he gave the first detailed description of scabies and of a polypoid colorectal tumour; 'first' claims in medical history are often disputed, say 'one of the first'.
use_in: Reel: 'He tested it on a goat first'

claim: During the Black Death, Ibn al-Khatib of Granada argued from what he saw that plague spread by contagion, at a time when many denied it.
evidence: determined that the bubonic plague was transmitted through contagion
source: Lapham's Quarterly contributor page; scholarly study: Ober WB, Aloush N. The plague at Granada, 1348-1349: Ibn al-Khatib and ideas of contagion. Bull N Y Acad Med 58(4): 418-424, 1982
locator: web page; article not yet read
author: Lapham's Quarterly; Ober & Aloush
caveat: Article text was blocked (captcha); read Ober & Aloush or Aberth, The Black Death (2005) pp. 114-116 for his own words before posting. He was later executed (1374), officially for heresy.
use_in: Reel: 'He said it was contagious. It cost him.' (check first)

claim: An 18th-century Timbuktu manuscript gives diagnoses and cures using plants, animals and minerals, alongside prayers.
evidence: The remedies described draw upon animal, plant, and mineral matter as well as prayers and Qur'anic verses.
source: The Met, 'Curing Diseases and Effects both Apparent and Hidden', Mali, Timbuktu, 18th century
author: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
licence: Met record text; image licence per object
caveat: HMML attributes the text Shifāʼ al-asqām to Aḥmad al-Raqqādī of the Kunta family (d. 1681 or 1684). Historical interest only, not medical advice. Some traditional remedies are toxic.

claim: Some Timbuktu medical handbooks name local trees in Bambara, and today's scholars cannot identify all of them. The knowledge is in the text, but the plant is lost.
evidence: Most entries include the names of local trees and plants (in Bambara, as well as other local languages)
source: Hill Museum & Manuscript Library, 'Medical Texts From Timbuktu: Local Pharmacological Remedies With Qur'anic Verses'
author: HMML
caveat: The article's example is a tree called Ṣukuru that the authors could not identify. Honest 'lost knowledge' angle, no 'ancient secret' framing.
use_in: Reel: 'Nobody knows which tree this is'

claim: A 2011 survey counted more than 100,000 manuscripts in at least 408 private family libraries in Mali.
evidence: A 2011 survey accounted for more than 100,000 such manuscripts preserved in no fewer than 408 private family libraries
author: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
caveat: Counts vary by survey; quote the Met's figure with its date.
use_in: Hook stat for the Timbuktu arc

claim: An enslaved West African man, Onesimus, told Cotton Mather how inoculation was done in Africa. In Boston's 1721 smallpox epidemic about 2% of inoculated people died versus about 14% of those who caught it naturally.
evidence: had undergone an Operation, which had given him something of the Small-Pox, and would forever preserve him from it
source: Cotton Mather, letter to the Royal Society, 1716, as quoted in Wikipedia 'Onesimus (Bostonian)'; numbers from Brown TH, JAMA 1988 and Boylston A, J R Soc Med 2012 ('The origins of inoculation')
author: Cotton Mather
caveat: Death figures differ by source (242 or 280 inoculated; ~2% vs ~14%). Check Boylston 2012 before posting. Mather owned Onesimus: tell it as Onesimus's knowledge, not Mather's. Inoculation (variolation) was risky and is no longer used.
use_in: Deep dive candidate: kindness + medicine + Free Minds

claim: The Ebers Papyrus, about 1550 BCE, is one of the oldest medical books known, with around 700 formulas and folk remedies.
evidence: The scroll contains 700 magical formulas and folk remedies meant to cure afflictions
author: Britannica
caveat: Counts vary (700 to 800+ prescriptions) by edition. Held at Leipzig University Library. Historical interest only, not medical advice. Some traditional remedies are toxic.

claim: Ethiopian healers kept handbooks that preserved and reused medical knowledge across generations; scholars study four such manuscripts in London and Paris.
evidence: The analysis shows how the specialist knowledge was transmitted, preserved and reused.
source: Burtea B. Traditional Medicine and Magic According to Some Ethiopian Manuscripts from European Collections. Aethiopica 18: 87-100, 2015
author: Bogdan Burtea
caveat: Abstract names no specific plants; read the article before posting remedies. Historical interest only, not medical advice. Some traditional remedies are toxic.
